extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and editors/translators of Euclid's Elements and classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Notes and critical commentary on Euclid's Elements focused on definitions, propositions, axioms, and editorial/translation decisions; guidance is aimed at producing a clear, rigorous edition and at teaching geometry. Includes recommended changes to enunciations, additions of corollaries, and remarks on omitted cases and necessary hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground definitions in the notion of a solid
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to consider a solid, that is, a magnitude which has length, breadth, and thickness, in order to understand aright the definitions of a point, line, and superficies; for these all arise from a solid, and exist in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of point, line, and superficies should be motivated and explained by their relation to solids (boundaries of solids and contiguous solids). The commentary unfolds why each has no thickness/breadth/length by thought experiments (removing adjacent solids/surfaces). Use such concrete grounding when presenting definitions to beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be precise and confined to their intended domain
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of angles and some others appears to attempt to include angles made by curves as well as straight lines; this causes ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous wording that mixes straight and curved lines. Keep definitions' domain and assumptions explicit (e.g., 'plane angle' meant for straight lines unless otherwise stated). If a definition's wording is unclear, either rephrase or mark as likely later/editorial addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit unnecessary conditions from definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: This definition has one condition more than is necessary; because every quadrilateral which has its opposite sides equal has likewise its opposite angles equal, and on the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not burden a definition with superfluous clauses that follow as corollaries. Keep definitions minimal and remove extraneous conditions that can be derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer demonstrable propositions over increasing axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition usually called the 5th postulate ... has given a great deal to do ... it seems not to be properly placed among the axioms, as it is not self-evident; but it may be demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, avoid introducing additional axioms unless truly self-evident; attempt to demonstrate propositions instead of elevating them to axioms, to keep the axiom set minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all necessary cases in propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two cases of this proposition, one of which is not in the Greek text, but is as necessary as the other ... the case left out has been formerly in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formulating and proving propositions, explicitly handle every distinct geometric case (different ordering/relative sizes, etc.). If the original text omits a case, reinstate or prove it to ensure completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add corollaries when they are necessary for later proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A corollary is added to this proposition, which is necessary to Prop. 1, B. 11, and otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include corollaries that are required for later arguments even if not present in the original source. Make dependencies explicit so later proofs can reference them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify harsh literal translations for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: It was thought proper to change the enunciation of this 7th prop, so as to preserve the very same meaning; the literal translation from the Greek being extremely harsh, and difficult to be understood by beginners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In translating/editting, prioritize clarity and accessibility for learners over slavish literalness. Preserve meaning but reword awkward literal translations to readable English, especially in enunciations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag and remove later editor additions that don't belong to original
rubrics_metrics.description: These definitions ... are the additions of some less skilful editor: on which account, especially, since they are quite useless, these definitions are distinguished from the rest by inverted double commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing an edition, identify likely later interpolations or editor's additions and mark/omit them when they are unnecessary or harmful to the original structure. Use critical apparatus to indicate such choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a construction requires choice to avoid multiple cases, state the restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: To this is added, 'of the two sides DE, DF, let DE be that which is not greater than the other;' that is, take that side of the two ... which is not greater than the other, in order to make with it the angle EDG equal to BAG; because, without this restriction, there might be three different cases of the proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state selection conditions (e.g., choose the shorter of two sides) to eliminate ambiguous multiple-case split in constructions and proofs, or else treat all cases separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain determinations underlying constructions (e.g., why circles meet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors blame Euclid for not demonstrating that the two circles ... must cut one another: but this is very plain from the determination he has given, viz. that any two of the straight lines DF, FG, GH must be greater than the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a construction's feasibility might be questioned (e.g., whether two circles intersect), include a short determination or inequality argument (triangle inequality style) to justify it rather than leaving it implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and state necessary properties of planes and lines used in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of this definition as it is in the Greek copies, a more distinct one is given from a property of a plane superficies, which is manifestly supposed in the Elements, viz. that a straight line drawn from any point in a plane to any other in it is wholly in that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit any geometric properties (like 'line between two points in a plane lies wholly within that plane') that are tacitly assumed in proofs, so the logical dependencies are visible to readers and beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define new terms used in arguments precisely (e.g., distance, nearer/further)
rubrics_metrics.description: DEFINITION 1. The distance of a point from a straight line, is the perpendicular drawn to it from the point. DEF. 2. One straight line is said to go nearer to, or further from, another straight line, when the distance of the points of the first from the other straight line become less or greater than they were.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce precise definitions for any notion used in proofs (distance, nearer/further, keeping same distance), because they form the basis of subsequent axioms and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt clear axioms for intuitive geometric behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: AXIOM. A straight line cannot first come nearer to another straight line, and then go further from it, before it cuts it; and in like manner, a straight line cannot go further from another straight line, and then come nearer to it; nor can a straight line keep the same distance from another straight line, and then come nearer to it, or go further from it; for a straight line keeps always the same direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate axioms capturing intuitive monotonic geometric behavior (used in proofs by contradiction). Present such axioms explicitly and illustrate them with simple figures to avoid hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contradiction with axioms and earlier props in elementary proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Example proofs (Prop. 1 & 2) argue by assuming inequality and using the axiom about nearer/further to derive impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving basic geometric equalities, a proof-by-contradiction that invokes earlier axioms (e.g., monotonic distance axiom) and previously proved propositions is acceptable and useful for clarity; show the impossibility step clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When bisecting or iterating constructions, justify limit/selection arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: If then the circumference BE be bisected, and its half again bisected, and so on, there will at length be left a circumference less than the circumference which is subtended by a straight line equal to GU inscribed in the circle BCDE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using iterative bisection or limit-style selection arguments in constructions, state the intended limiting outcome and justify why the process yields the required element (e.g., a chord shorter than a given length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why added or omitted parts create dependency or are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The second part of prop. 5 was added upon account of prop. 7 ... this part must therefore have been added to prop. 5, upon account of some proposition betwixt the 5th and 13th, but none of these stand in need of it except the 7th proposition, on account of which it has been added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editorial additions are made, document the reason — e.g., to supply a dependency needed by a later proposition — so readers understand why the text differs from earlier manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a supposedly 'manifest' truth is used, still provide reasoning if it reduces axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Proclus relates that the Epicureans derided this proposition, as being manifest even to asses, and needing no demonstration; his answer is, that though the truth of it be manifest to our senses, yet it is science which must give the reason why two sides of a triangle are greater than the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for statements apparent by sight, include a formal demonstration when that reduces the need for additional axioms and strengthens the deductive structure of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about diagrammatic positions (e.g., point falls below line) when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Thomas Simpson ... observes ... that it ought to have been shown that the point F falls below the line EG; this probably Euclid omitted as it is very easy to perceive...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a diagrammatic relation (point above/below a line) is used in a proof, either demonstrate it or at least state it explicitly to prevent ambiguity for readers who might draw different configurations.
